topic.subject: social
topic.title: Working of institutions
topic.scope: President, Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, Parliament, Supreme Court, bureaucracy

misconceptions.statement: The Rajya Sabha is more powerful than the Lok Sabha because it is the Upper House.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the term 'Upper' with 'higher authority' or 'greater power'.
misconceptions.fix: The Lok Sabha is more powerful because its members are directly elected and it controls the budget and the government's survival.

probe.question: If the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha disagree on a normal bill, whose decision prevails?

misconceptions.statement: The Prime Minister is the head of the country.
misconceptions.why: Media focus on the PM as the face of the government leads to conflating the head of government with the head of state.
misconceptions.fix: The President is the head of state, while the Prime Minister is the head of government.

probe.question: Who is the official Head of State in India?

misconceptions.root_belief: The most visible person is the most powerful.

misconceptions.statement: Civil servants make the final decisions on government policy.
misconceptions.why: Students see bureaucrats implementing laws and assume they are the ones who created them.
misconceptions.fix: Civil servants assist in policy implementation, but the final decision-making power rests with the elected political executive.

probe.question: Who takes the final decision on a policy proposal?

misconceptions.root_belief: Those who do the work have the authority.
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver children's ideas in social studies

misconceptions.statement: The Supreme Court can change any law passed by Parliament at any time.
misconceptions.why: Students overgeneralize the concept of judicial review, ignoring the constitutional limitations.
misconceptions.fix: The Supreme Court can only declare a law invalid if it violates the basic structure or provisions of the Constitution.

probe.question: Can the Supreme Court strike down any law it dislikes?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it has the power to change any law.

misconceptions.statement: Members of Parliament are chosen by the people for both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha in the same way.
misconceptions.why: Students know that Parliament is 'elected by the people' and assume both Houses are filled by the same direct voting.
misconceptions.fix: Lok Sabha members are directly elected by the people from constituencies. Rajya Sabha members are indirectly elected by the elected members (MLAs) of State Legislative Assemblies.

probe.question: Who elects the members of the Rajya Sabha?
probe.wrong_answer: All the voting citizens of India elect them directly, as they elect Lok Sabha members.

misconceptions.root_belief: Both Houses are filled by identical direct elections

misconceptions.statement: The President is not a part of Parliament; Parliament means only the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.
misconceptions.why: Students picture Parliament as the two Houses with seats and debates, and see the President as a separate ceremonial office.
misconceptions.fix: Parliament consists of the President and the two Houses, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. A bill becomes a law only after the President gives assent.

probe.question: Name the parts that together make up the Indian Parliament.
probe.wrong_answer: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha only.

misconceptions.root_belief: Parliament equals only the houses where debates happen

misconceptions.statement: A bill passed by both Houses of Parliament becomes a law automatically.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on voting in Parliament as the end of the law-making process and ignore the final step.
misconceptions.fix: After both Houses pass a bill, it goes to the President. It becomes a law only when the President gives assent.

probe.question: What must happen after both Houses pass a bill before it becomes a law?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing more is needed; it becomes a law as soon as both Houses vote for it.

misconceptions.root_belief: Voting in the legislature alone completes law-making

misconceptions.statement: The Rajya Sabha can reject a Money Bill passed by the Lok Sabha.
misconceptions.why: Students generalise that each House has an equal veto over bills, so the second House can stop any bill.
misconceptions.fix: A Money Bill is introduced only in the Lok Sabha. The Rajya Sabha can only give recommendations, which the Lok Sabha may accept or ignore, and it cannot block the bill.

probe.question: If the Rajya Sabha disagrees with a Money Bill passed by the Lok Sabha, what can it do?
probe.wrong_answer: It can reject the bill and stop it from becoming a law.

misconceptions.root_belief: Both Houses have equal veto over every bill

misconceptions.statement: Lok Sabha members are elected by the people, so the Lok Sabha can be dissolved but the Rajya Sabha can also be dissolved.
misconceptions.why: Students think every legislative body is dissolved and re-elected together after five years.
misconceptions.fix: The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House and is never dissolved as a whole. One-third of its members retire every two years. The Lok Sabha is elected for five years and can be dissolved.

probe.question: What happens to the Rajya Sabha when a new Lok Sabha is elected after five years?
probe.wrong_answer: It is dissolved too and all its members are elected afresh.

misconceptions.root_belief: All legislative bodies share the same fixed term

misconceptions.statement: The Prime Minister is appointed by the President by personal choice, so the President can pick anyone.
misconceptions.why: Students read 'the President appoints the Prime Minister' literally and miss the role of the Lok Sabha majority.
misconceptions.fix: The President appoints the leader of the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha as Prime Minister. The President cannot choose freely.

probe.question: On what basis does the President appoint the Prime Minister?
probe.wrong_answer: The President selects whichever person they think is best.

misconceptions.root_belief: Formal appointment means free personal choice by appointer

misconceptions.statement: Ministers are permanent executive and stay in office even after elections are lost.
misconceptions.why: Students see ministers and civil servants both running departments and assume both hold their posts for a fixed long period.
misconceptions.fix: Ministers are the political executive, elected for a term and removed when their party loses. Civil servants are the permanent executive, appointed on merit, and stay in office even when the government changes.

probe.question: Who continues to work in the ministry after a new party forms the government?
probe.wrong_answer: The old ministers, because ministers are the permanent executive.

misconceptions.root_belief: All people running government departments have equal tenure

misconceptions.statement: Judges are appointed and can be removed by the government whenever it wants.
misconceptions.why: Students assume that those who appoint can also dismiss, and that the government controls all institutions.
misconceptions.fix: Judges are appointed by the President in consultation with the Chief Justice, and a judge can be removed only by an impeachment process in Parliament. This keeps the judiciary independent.

probe.question: If the government is unhappy with a judge's verdict, can it remove the judge?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the government can dismiss the judge at any time.

misconceptions.root_belief: Appointing authority has unlimited power to dismiss
